title: Do Verifiers Reduce Security-Relevant Misconfigurations? A Preregistered Paired Evaluation of Verifier-in-the-Loop GVR for Intent-to-Configuration
abstract: We preregistered and executed a deterministic paired experiment (N = 300 matched intents) to test whether embedding a reachability/policy verifier inside a generate–verify–repair (GVR) loop reduces security-increasing (forbidden-reachability) misconfigurations produced by an LLM-driven intent→configuration pipeline. Using Dockerized FRRouting-style emulation, two deterministic validators combined with a logical-OR decision rule, and a shared_initial_candidate generation contract (one LLM candidate replayed to both arms), the run completed all planned episodes with model_calls_used = 300. Confirmatory outcome: baseline_success_count = 300 and guarded_success_count = 300 (contingency n11 = 300, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0); McNemar exact two-sided p = 1.0; bootstrap 95% CI for the paired risk-difference = [0.0, 0.0] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729). Because validators never detected forbidden reachability, no repair call was invoked and the confirmatory hypothesis about repair efficacy was not testable in this run; a one-sided Clopper–Pearson 95% upper bound on an undetected baseline violation rate ≈ 0.00994. We release the preregistration and deterministic per-episode artifacts to support reproducibility and to document design lessons for follow-up stress tests that intentionally exercise the repair path.

sections.introduction: LLM-based intent-to-configuration systems promise to reduce operator workload but raise operational-security concerns: generated artifacts can inadvertently expand attack surface or violate access-control and routing policies. Prior system and survey work therefore recommends verifier-assisted or execution-guided repair loops as mitigations. We pursued a focused, preregistered, paired evaluation question: Does embedding a reachability/policy verifier inside a GVR loop reduce the incidence of forbidden-reachability misconfigurations produced by an LLM-driven pipeline when exposed to programmatic adversarial variants? Our contributions are: (1) a machine-readable preregistration fixing a paired N = 300 confirmatory design (cnd-2026-netops-gvr-security-01-prereg-v1); (2) deterministic Dockerized execution with two complementary validators and explicit shared_initial_candidate semantics to conserve model calls; (3) complete, artifact-grounded execution and analysis showing a degenerate confirmatory outcome (n11 = 300) with numerical bounds on undetected violation rates; and (4) artifact-grounded design lessons and prescriptive recommendations for follow-up stress tests that exercise verifier-guided repair.
sections.related_work: Three strands motivate the study. First, generate–verify–repair and execution-guided repair architectures improve correctness for code and IaC tasks by using execution traces or verifier feedback to direct repair; system papers (e.g., TerraFormer) show verifier strength and repair strategy determine realized gains [doi:10.1145/3786583.3786898]. Second, surveys and NetOps system research document LLM failure modes (hallucination, overconfidence, domain mismatch) and consistently recommend validators, constrained generation, or human oversight to reduce risk [https://openalex.org/W4415071524; https://openalex.org/W4404602270]. Third, emulator/testbed work demonstrates practical execution-based validation but cautions about external-validity gaps when porting to production devices [https://openalex.org/W4406170828]. Our experiment fills a narrow, preregistered, reproducibility-focused niche: a paired confirmatory design with deterministic validators and explicit generation semantics to quantify whether verifier insertion changes observed compliance under the chosen contract.
sections.methodology: Design and preregistration: The preregistration (cnd-2026-netops-gvr-security-01-prereg-v1) specified a paired binary design with N = 300 matched intents (150 benign seeds and 150 programmatic adversarial variants), an exact McNemar two-sided confirmatory test (alpha = 0.05) on the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline estimand, and prespecified bootstrap percentile CIs. Sampling and deduplication followed the preregistered rules (exact duplicates and fuzzy duplicates with normalized edit distance < 0.15 removed). Execution contract and generation semantics: to limit provider usage the study used shared_initial_candidate semantics: for each pair a single initial LLM candidate was generated and replayed to both arms (baseline = replayed candidate; guarded = replayed candidate + verifier check + up to one repair call if any validator reported forbidden reachability). This choice yields model_calls_used = 300 for 300 pairs (instead of up to 600 for independent draws) and is explicitly recorded in the execution manifest. Scoring and validators: two deterministic validators were used and combined with a logical-OR decision rule (a pair is labeled 'violating' if any validator reports the forbidden-reachability predicate). The preregistration and execution records identify the validators as: (a) a containerized Batfish-style execution validator that performs concrete execution/emulation checks (routing, forwarding and ACL/policy behavior under the Dockerized FRR environment), and (b) a lightweight Python graph-based static reachability analyzer that computes abstract forwarding/reachability implications from device/interface state and declared policies. Forbidden-reachability predicate (concise operational definition): For this study we operationalized a violation as any validator-detected breach of the preregistered forbidden-reachability predicate encoded in the task payload workflow_policies (examples: access to protected interfaces listed under task payload 'protected_interfaces', or explicit workflow constraints such as group/activity constraints and must_be_down_for_fields). In other words, a configuration is flagged if it enables reachability or policy outcomes disallowed by the task's workflow_policies. Validator assumptions and failure modes: the execution validator assumes deterministic FRR-like forwarding and evaluates concrete forwarding/ACL semantics in the emulated environment; it can miss environment-level dynamics not captured in the emulator. The static analyzer approximates forwarding via graph reachability and can produce false negatives where dynamic policy interactions or stateful behaviors matter. These assumptions and per-episode validator_trace outputs are archived for independent assessment. Repair policy and budget: repair calls were allowed only when a validator detected forbidden reachability, with at most one repair LLM call per pair (preregistered). Analysis: primary test used exact McNemar; bootstrap percentile 95% CIs computed with 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729). Sensitivity analyses for technical failures were prespecified; no technical failures occurred.
sections.results: Execution accounting: planned episodes = 600 (300 pairs × 2 arms); completed = 600; failed episodes = 0. Provider-call accounting under shared_initial_candidate: model_calls_used = 300. Primary outcomes: baseline_success_count = 300; guarded_success_count = 300; contingency: n11 = 300, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0 (Table 1). Paired risk-difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0; exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0. Bootstrap 95% percentile CI (10,000 resamples, seed 1729) for the paired risk-difference = [0.0, 0.0]. Because no validator detected forbidden reachability on any initial candidate, no repair call was invoked (repair_applied = false for all archived scoring traces) and verifier_disagreement_rate = 0 across the two validators on the recorded episodes. Interpretation: the observed degenerate contingency (all concordant passes) makes the McNemar paired test uninformative about repair efficacy because there are no discordant pairs to compare. Observing 0/300 violations yields a one-sided Clopper–Pearson 95% upper bound on the baseline violation probability ≈ 0.00994; this bound is reported as a descriptive constraint on undetected baseline violations. Representative verification pointers: the primary numeric artifacts supporting these results are archived (examples: analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv and analysis/condition_summary.csv) together with per-episode validator_trace entries; the full artifact bundle is archived for independent verification.
sections.discussion: What the evidence supports: under the declared model (gpt-5-mini), the Dockerized FRR-style emulator, the two deterministic validators combined by logical OR, and the shared_initial_candidate contract, baseline generation produced no validator-detected forbidden-reachability violations; therefore inserting the verifier did not change observed compliance. What the evidence does not show: because the repair path was never exercised, this experiment provides no evidence that verifier-guided repair can rescue violating initial candidates. Design lessons grounded in the artifacts: (1) generation semantics strongly affect inferential power—shared_initial_candidate conserves model calls but reduces independent-sample variance needed to produce discordant violating outputs; to exercise repair efficacy use independent-condition generation (two draws per pair) or increase the repair-call budget, noting that this will raise model-call costs (the execution manifest documents the maximum_model_calls = 600 budgetary ceiling); (2) adversary potency matters—the programmatic adversarial variants used here did not trigger validator-detectable violations for this model/validator configuration, so stronger or targeted adversaries are required to stress repair paths; (3) verifier diversity and oracle strength matter—combining execution and static analyzers provided concordant negative results here, but production-grade oracles and richer dynamic checks may expose vulnerabilities missed in this emulation. Threats to validity: internal validity limited by shared_initial_candidate semantics and single-model scope; construct validity depends on whether the implemented forbidden-reachability predicate and the two validators adequately capture operational security risk; external validity is limited by synthetic tasks and deterministic emulation; conclusion validity is constrained because the observed contingency is degenerate and original power assumptions (nonzero baseline violation rate) were not met.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered paired evaluation of a verifier-in-the-loop GVR pipeline using deterministic validators and a shared_initial_candidate generation contract. The run completed N = 300 matched pairs with model_calls_used = 300 and produced n11 = 300 (both arms passed the forbidden-reachability predicate for all pairs). Because validators never reported violations, no repair calls were made and the experiment cannot assess whether verifier-guided repair rescues violations. The principal operational contribution is deterministic execution accounting, transparent per-episode validator traces, and concrete design lessons (generation semantics, adversary potency, repair budget, verifier strength) to guide follow-up stress tests that intentionally exercise the repair path. We archive the preregistration and the per-episode artifacts to facilitate replication and targeted follow-up experiments.

limitations: Degenerate confirmatory outcome: zero discordant pairs (n11 = 300, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0) render McNemar inference uninformative about repair efficacy when baseline violation rates are nonzero; the preregistered power calculation assumed a nonzero baseline violation rate and targeted detecting a 30 percentage-point absolute reduction.

GVR not exercised: under the chosen task set, emulator, model, and validators the verifier never reported forbidden reachability and consequently the guarded repair step was never invoked; the experiment therefore tests whether verifier insertion changes compliance when baseline is already compliant, not whether verifier-guided repair rescues violations.

Generation contract choice: the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics produced one LLM call per pair and reduced model-call overhead but also limited independent draws that could produce discordant errors; alternative contracts (independent-condition generation or expanded repair budgets) would better exercise repair paths.

Adversarial-perturbation detail: the preregistration specified programmatic generation of one adversarial variant per benign seed; per-task generation seeds and intent payloads are archived in execution/task_manifest.jsonl and the transformation logs are available in the execution manifest for reproducibility.

External validity: tasks were synthetically generated and executed in Dockerized FRRouting-style emulation; results do not necessarily generalize to heterogeneous production devices, live traffic conditions, or different operational constraints.
Model and verifier scope: a single model (gpt-5-mini) and two deterministic validators were evaluated; other LLMs, stronger verifiers, or dynamic execution oracles may produce different outcomes.
